blocks.h: 1. a) What a general average act is

blocks.p: General average is the principle that where one interest is deliberately sacrificed to save the whole, the loss is shared rateably by all the interests saved. It is given effect not by statute but by the York-Antwerp Rules, incorporated by contract; the current edition is the 2016 Rules. In India the statutory definition appears in section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act 1963.

Rule A states the test: there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure. The words when, and only when matter - the conditions are cumulative.

blocks.h: 2. The essential features, all of which must be present

ol: Extraordinary - outside the ordinary incidents of the voyage. Fuel burnt on a normal passage, or wear and tear, is not; nor is anything the owner was already bound to do.

Intentional - a deliberate act. This is the heart of the doctrine: accidental loss, however catastrophic, is never general average. Cargo washed overboard is particular average; cargo jettisoned is general average.

Reasonable - judged on the circumstances as they appeared at the time, reinforced by the Rule Paramount: in no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred.
For the common safety - for the whole adventure. Action to save only the ship, or only the cargo, is not general average.
A real peril - real and substantial, though it need not be immediate or inevitable.

A common maritime adventure, and a useful result - more than one interest at risk, or there is nobody to contribute, and something must be saved, since contribution is assessed on the values preserved.

blocks.h: 3. What is excluded, and who must prove it

ul: Rule C allows only the direct consequence of the general average act, and excludes demurrage, loss of market, any loss or expense by reason of delay and any indirect loss whatsoever, and environmental damage or loss consequent on the escape of pollutants.

Rule D - rights to contribution are not affected though the event was due to the fault of a party, without prejudice to remedies or defences for that fault. Contribution and liability are separate questions.
Rule E - the onus of proof is on the party claiming; failing particulars within twelve months the adjuster may estimate.

blocks.h: 4. b) Testing the casualty against the rules

blocks.p: Taking the Rule A elements against the facts - aground, the main engine worked ahead and astern to move her from the ground, bearings burnt through excessive load:

ul: extraordinary - burnt bearings from deliberate overload are outside the ordinary incidents of the voyage, and are not wear and tear;
intentional - working the engine hard astern to refloat is a deliberate act of the master;
for the common safety - a grounded vessel endangers ship, cargo and freight alike;
direct consequence - the damage arose immediately from that act, satisfying Rule C;
peril - the one element the question does not settle, and it must be examined rather than assumed.

blocks.h: 5. Rule VII, which decides the point

blocks.p: The Rules deal with this precise situation expressly. Rule VII, Damage to Machinery and Boilers: Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.

Three conditions and one absolute bar. The conditions: ashore; in a position of peril; machinery worked with an actual intention to float her for the common safety, at the risk of such damage. The bar: if she is afloat, machinery damage from working the engines is never allowed.

blocks.h: 6. Conclusion, and what must be done to sustain it

blocks.p: Yes - the bearing damage can be included in general average, provided the Rule VII conditions are established. The first is satisfied: she was aground. The other two are questions of evidence:

ul: Position of peril. Hard aground on a falling tide, on a lee shore or on rock, taking water, or with weather deteriorating - peril is readily shown. Merely touching soft ground in sheltered water, certain to float on the next tide, is not; the act was one of convenience and the claim fails.

Actual intention, accepting the risk. The master must have worked the engine knowing it might be damaged and accepted that to free the ship. Engines worked to test the ground, or in routine hope of coming off, do not meet the rule.

Evidence. Timed deck and engine log entries, the master's recorded assessment of the danger, engine parameters and alarms, soundings, weather, owner or salvor advice. The onus is on the claimant under Rule E.

blocks.p: Two points complete the answer. The damage must be reasonable in extent under the Rule Paramount. And by Rule D, negligent navigation causing the grounding does not lose the right to contribution, though cargo may resist under the contract of carriage. In practice the owner declares general average, appoints an average adjuster and releases cargo against a general average bond and an average guarantee.

Limb (b) is worth 8 marks and asks for justification, which means the marks are in the reasoning chain, not the verdict. An answer that says 'yes, it is general average because the engine was used to save the ship' has given the conclusion and none of the justification. Running the Rule A elements first and then reaching Rule VII lets the candidate show the general test and the specific rule, and - crucially - identify the two facts the question deliberately leaves open.

blocks.h: The question is testing whether you know Rule VII exists

blocks.p: This scenario is not a general knowledge problem; it is drafted straight onto a named rule. Every element in the stem maps to a phrase in Rule VII: ran aground to 'ashore', main engine used ahead and astern to move the vessel from the ground to 'in endeavouring to refloat', bearings got burnt to 'damage caused to any machinery'. A candidate who cites Rule A alone can reach the right answer by general reasoning and will score respectably; one who cites Rule VII and quotes the afloat proviso is demonstrably answering the question that was set.

blocks.h: Why the law inverts ordinary intuition

blocks.p: The rule that deliberate damage is recoverable and accidental damage is not looks perverse until you see what it is for. General average is a cost-allocation mechanism, not a compensation scheme. Its purpose is to remove the master's conflict of interest at the moment of crisis: if the shipowner alone bore the cost of sacrificing the ship's machinery, or of jettisoning cargo, the person best placed to save the adventure would have a financial reason to hesitate. By promising that a reasonable, deliberate sacrifice will be shared by everyone who benefits, the doctrine makes the right decision the cheap decision. Accidental loss needs no such encouragement, which is why it stays where it falls.

blocks.h: The afloat proviso, and why it is absolute

blocks.p: Rule VII's second half is unusually emphatic - in any circumstances. The reason is evidential rather than moral. When a ship is afloat, working the propelling machinery is exactly what she is supposed to do, so there is no way to distinguish an extraordinary sacrifice from ordinary use, and a claim would be unanswerable and unverifiable. When she is ashore, the act is visibly abnormal and the intention can be tested. The Rules solve the evidential problem by drawing a bright line.

ul: Concluding 'no' because the damage was caused by overload. Overload was the mechanism; the question is whether it was accepted deliberately, in peril, to refloat.
Concluding 'yes' unconditionally, without identifying peril and intention as things to be proved.
Citing only Rule A when Rule VII is directly on point.
Forgetting the afloat proviso, which is half of Rule VII and the source of the best follow-up question.
Saying negligence defeats general average. Rule D says it does not - it may found a separate claim.
Confusing general average with salvage or with particular average.
Calling the York-Antwerp Rules a convention or statute. They are contractual terms.
The stem says a large vessel ran aground and stops. It does not say she was in peril, and that omission is deliberate - it is the fact the answer must treat as conditional.
'Give proper justification' is a direction about form. A bare verdict cannot score, however correct.

Limb (a) is a quotation - 'General average is based on certain essential features' - and quotation stems reward candidates who enumerate the features explicitly rather than writing an essay around them.
Same damage, but the vessel is afloat and working engines against a gale to hold off a lee shore. General average?

blocks.p: Learn Rule A as a sentence - every essential feature is one of its words, so the definition and the list are the same thing. For the applied limb, hold Rule VII as four conditions and one bar: ashore, in peril, intending to float, accepting the risk - never if afloat. And hold the one-line principle that answers most general average scenarios: somebody must have chosen it, on purpose, for everybody.

Rule Paramount - no allowance unless reasonably made or incurred.
Rule C - direct consequence only; delay, demurrage, loss of market, indirect loss and environmental damage excluded.
Rule D - fault does not affect the right to contribution.
Rule E - onus on the claimant; twelve-month particulars.
Rule VII - damage to machinery and boilers in refloating. Decides limb (b).

blocks.p: The York-Antwerp Rules are contractual, not statutory: they apply because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, and which edition applies is therefore a question about the contract. The 2016 edition was read and is cited here. Rule VII is materially unchanged across the 1994, 2004 and 2016 editions, so the conclusion in limb (b) does not depend on the choice - but the answer states the dependency rather than assuming it. Section 66 of the Indian Marine Insurance Act 1963 is cited as a pointer to the Indian statutory position; it was not read in the statute for this question and the answer does not rest on its wording. Note for candidates that the Indian Act is the 1963 Act, not the English Marine Insurance Act 1906.

quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) Rule A, York-Antwerp Rules: 'There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.' The essential features are cumulative: extraordinary, not an ordinary incident of the voyage; intentional, a deliberate act and not an accident; reasonable, reinforced by the Rule Paramount that there is no allowance unless reasonably made or incurred; for the common safety, so more than one interest must be at risk; a real peril; and a useful result, since there must be property left to contribute. Rule C allows only direct consequences and excludes delay, demurrage, loss of market, indirect loss, and environmental damage or pollutant escape. Rule D preserves the right to contribution even where the casualty was somebody's fault, without prejudice to remedies for that fault. Rule E puts the onus of proof on the party claiming. (b) Yes, allowable - subject to proof, and the governing provision is Rule VII, Damage to Machinery and Boilers: damage to machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, is allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where the ship is afloat, no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers is in any circumstances allowed. So the burnt bearings qualify if the vessel was genuinely in peril and the engine was worked with that intention, accepting the risk - both questions of evidence, proved from the log, engine records and the master's recorded decision.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: York-Antwerp Rules, Rule A and Rule VII, with the Rule Paramount and Rules C, D and E; in India the statutory definition of a general average loss is in section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act 1963.
quick_revision.major_trap: Two traps, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is treating any serious casualty damage as general average - accidental damage is never general average, however severe. The second, in this scenario, is refusing the claim because the engine was damaged by overload: Rule VII expressly allows machinery damage sustained in refloating, provided the ship was ashore and in a position of peril and the engine was worked with an actual intention to float her for the common safety at the risk of such damage. If she had been afloat, the same damage could never be allowed.

questions.understand_first: General average is the one place in marine practice where deliberately damaging your own ship can be recovered, and accidental damage cannot. That inversion is the whole subject. If a bearing fails on passage through overload, it is the owner's loss alone; if the same bearing is burnt because the master knowingly drove the engine hard to save the ship and cargo from a common danger, every interest that was saved contributes to it. So when a scenario asks whether damage is general average, do not ask how bad it was - ask whether somebody chose it, on purpose, for everybody's benefit.
questions.memory_cue: The features are a gate every claim must pass - extraordinary, intentional, reasonable, common, peril, result (step 2). Then in limb (b) one rule decides it: ashore, in peril, intending to float, accepting the risk (step 5) - and never if afloat.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the general average question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a general average act is. 2 The essential features. 3 Exclusions and onus. 4 Testing the casualty. 5 Rule VII, which decides it. 6 Conclusion and what must be proved.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 3 are the 8-mark doctrine limb, steps 4 to 6 the 8-mark applied limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the Rule A definition of a general average act.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: Every essential feature is a word in this sentence, so learning the sentence gives you the list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does York-Antwerp Rule VII provide about damage to machinery and boilers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage to machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, is allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage. Where the ship is afloat, no damage from working the propelling machinery and boilers is in any circumstances allowed.
retrieval_cards.why: This single rule decides the whole of limb (b), including the reason the answer would be different if she were afloat.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is accidental damage never general average, however severe?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because Rule A requires the sacrifice to be made intentionally. General average shares the cost of a deliberate choice made for everyone's benefit; an accident is nobody's choice and falls where it lies, as particular average.
retrieval_cards.why: The inversion - deliberate damage recoverable, accidental damage not - is the single idea the topic rests on.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Under Rule D, does it matter that the grounding was caused by the owner's or crew's negligence?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rights to contribution in general average are not affected even though the event was due to the fault of a party to the adventure, without prejudice to any remedies or defences available in respect of that fault.
retrieval_cards.why: Contribution and liability are separate questions, and candidates routinely collapse them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the shipowner prove to sustain a Rule VII claim for the burnt bearings?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the vessel was ashore and in a position of peril; that the engine was worked in endeavouring to refloat her; that this was done with an actual intention to float her for the common safety, accepting the risk of such damage; and that the damage was the direct consequence. The onus is on the claimant under Rule E.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asks for justification, and the justification is a list of things to be evidenced, not an assertion.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the practical steps once general average is declared?
retrieval_cards.answer: The owner declares general average and appoints an average adjuster; cargo is released against a general average bond from receivers and an average guarantee from their underwriters, or a cash deposit; the adjuster collects values and particulars and issues the statement apportioning the loss over the contributing interests.
retrieval_cards.why: The commercial machinery is what turns a legal entitlement into money, and it is a standard oral follow-up.

blocks.h: 1. Which text applies, and how the Convention is built

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 is an ILO instrument which entered into force on 20 August 2013 and is generally described as the fourth pillar of the international regulatory regime, alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW.
Say how it is built, because all four limbs of this question sit inside that structure:

ul: Articles - the treaty obligations of the Member;
Regulations - the substantive requirements;
Code Part A - Standards, which are mandatory;
Code Part B - Guidelines, which are guidance to be given due consideration.
Five Titles, of which Title 5 is compliance and enforcement and divides into flag State, port State and labour-supplying responsibilities - the same three-way split this question follows.

blocks.p: One temporal point belongs at the top. At this sitting the operative text is the Convention as amended through the 2022 amendments - the amendments approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session in 2022, in force since 23 December 2024 - among them access to social connectivity, free drinking water, appropriately sized personal protective equipment, strengthened food and catering provisions, and the repatriation of the remains of a seafarer who dies on board. The amendments approved by the 113th Session of the International Labour Conference on 6 June 2025 - among them shore leave without a visa or special permit, and recognition of seafarers as key workers - are adopted but not in force; their expected entry into force is 23 December 2027. Nothing from that set is a present obligation.

blocks.h: (a) Flag State and port State responsibilities
2. Flag State and port State responsibilities

blocks.p: Flag State. The flag State must establish an effective system of inspection and certification of labour conditions, ensuring that ships flying its flag comply.

ul: It may authorise recognized organizations to carry out inspection and certification, but it remains fully responsible for the work done on its behalf, must satisfy itself of their competence and independence, and must make the list public.

Ships of 500 gross tonnage and over on international voyages, or operating from or between foreign ports, must carry a Maritime Labour Certificate and a Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance; others may be certified on request.

The DMLC is in two parts, and the split is the classic examination point. Part I is drawn up by the competent authority and identifies the national requirements; Part II is drawn up by the shipowner and sets out the measures adopted on the ship to ensure ongoing compliance.
The certificate is valid for five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates; an interim certificate may be issued for six months.

The interval between inspections shall in no case exceed three years. Inspectors must be qualified and independent, must report to the authority and the master, and have power to require rectification and to prohibit the ship from sailing until deficiencies are put right.

blocks.p: Port State. Any foreign ship calling in the port of a Member may be inspected to determine compliance.

ul: But the certificate and the DMLC must be accepted as prima facie evidence of compliance, so the ordinary inspection is a document review. Without that presumption the certificate would be worth nothing and every port would re-audit every ship.
The port State inspection is limited to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A of the Code - the mandatory material. Part B Guidelines are not the measure of compliance.

No more favourable treatment. A ship flying the flag of a State that has not ratified the Convention is entitled to no better treatment than one that has - which is what stops non-ratification from becoming a commercial advantage.
Where more is needed, the officer proceeds to a more detailed inspection, which is limb (c).

blocks.p: Every ship must carry on-board procedures for the fair, effective and expeditious handling of seafarer complaints alleging breaches of the Convention.

ul: The design preference is resolution at the lowest level - the complaint is raised with the head of department and worked upward.

But that preference is expressly without prejudice to the seafarer's right to complain directly to the master, and to complain directly to external authorities - the flag State administration, or an authorized officer in a port of call. A procedure that required him to exhaust the chain of command first would not comply.

A copy of the procedures must be provided to every seafarer, together with contact information for the competent authority of the flag State and of the seafarer's country of residence, and the name of a person on board who can advise him impartially and otherwise assist him.
The seafarer has the right to be accompanied or represented during the procedure.
Victimization for filing a complaint is prohibited and must be penalized. This is the provision that makes everything else usable: without it the machinery exists and nobody dares use it.

blocks.p: A seafarer may bring a complaint to an authorized officer in the port at which the ship has called. The procedure is an escalation with three rungs:

ul: Ship level first. The officer makes an initial investigation, and where the complaint can be resolved at ship level he seeks that resolution - the on-board procedure is used or reinstated, and where the complaint concerns matters within a more detailed inspection he proceeds accordingly.

Flag State next. If it cannot be resolved on board, the officer notifies the flag State, seeking advice and a corrective plan of action, with a deadline. A copy of the report goes to the shipowners' and seafarers' organisations in the port State.

The ILO last. Where the matter remains unresolved, the port State sends a copy of the report, with the flag State's response, to the Director-General of the International Labour Office, so that the failure is recorded internationally.

The source of the complaint is kept confidential at every stage, and the officer must take appropriate steps to safeguard it - including giving no intimation to the master or the owner that an inspection was made on account of a complaint.

blocks.h: (c) Detainable deficiencies under flag State and port State intervention
5. Detainable deficiencies under flag State and port State intervention

blocks.p: Begin with what the Convention does not do. Unlike the regional port State control memoranda, the MLC publishes no list of detainable deficiencies. It states two grounds, and a candidate who recites a memorandum's list has answered from the wrong instrument.
Port State intervention - the two grounds. A foreign ship may be detained where the conditions on board are shown, following a more detailed inspection, to be:

ul: clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers; or
a serious or repeated breach of the requirements of the Convention, including seafarers' rights.

blocks.p: Flag State intervention uses the same two grounds. The flag State's inspectors may require deficiencies to be remedied and, where they have grounds to believe that deficiencies are a serious breach of the Convention, including seafarers' rights, or a significant danger to seafarers' safety, health or security, they may prohibit the ship from leaving port until the necessary action is taken (Standard A5.1.4). The difference is reach: the flag State can stop its own ship in any port; the port State can detain a foreign ship only after a more detailed inspection.

The route to them matters as much as the grounds themselves. Detention is reached only through a more detailed inspection, and that inspection may be carried out only where one of four triggers is present:

ul: the required documents are not produced, or are not maintained, or are falsely maintained, or do not contain the information required;
there are clear grounds for believing the working and living conditions do not conform;
there are reasonable grounds to believe the ship changed flag to avoid compliance;
there is a complaint alleging that specific conditions do not conform.

blocks.p: What follows a finding.

ul: The deficiencies are to be rectified; or, where rectification cannot be completed in that port, the officer may accept a plan of action with a timetable.
The ship is not released until the hazard is removed or the plan accepted.
The flag State is notified forthwith, and the shipowners' and seafarers' organisations in the port State are informed.

Compensation is payable for any loss or damage suffered where a ship is unduly detained or delayed. The Convention places the burden of proof in each case on the complainant, and that provision is the discipline on the inspector.

blocks.h: (d) Grievance redressal mechanisms for Indian seafarers

blocks.p: Answer this in three layers, because a single list would hide the point.

Layer 1 - the Convention's own route, which every Indian seafarer already has. India is a ratifying Member, so the whole of the machinery in limbs (b) and (c) is available to him: the on-board procedure with its impartial adviser and its protection from victimization; direct complaint to the master; direct complaint to the flag State administration; complaint to an authorized officer in any port of a ratifying Member; and, at the end, the Director-General of the ILO.
Layer 2 - what India can actually reach, and this is the substance of the limb.

ul: For an Indian-flag ship, India is the flag State and the full inspection, certification and enforcement apparatus of Title 5 is Indian.

But most Indian seafarers serve on foreign-flag ships, where India is neither the flag State nor, usually, the port State. The operative head is then India's labour-supplying responsibility, which is the third limb of Title 5 and is the one that exists precisely for large seafarer-supplying countries.

Under it, and under the recruitment and placement provisions, India licenses and regulates crewing agents, requires registers to be kept and employment agreements to be verified, enforces the prohibition on charging recruitment fees to the seafarer - save for the statutory medical certificate, the seafarer's book and a passport - and requires a system of protection to compensate the seafarer for monetary loss arising from the agent's failure to meet its obligations.
That is where the practical remedy lies. The foreign owner is beyond India's reach; the agent who put the man on board is not.

blocks.p: Layer 3 - the domestic frame.

ul: The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, in force since 15 March 2026 (repealing the 1958 Act), is the statute through which India gives effect to its flag State, port State and labour-supplying obligations.
The shipping master is the officer concerned with engagement and discharge of seafarers and with disputes over wages arising from them.

The maritime administration is the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) - the Directorate General of Shipping as reconstituted under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. Its e-Navik portal carries a round-the-clock grievance redressal mechanism open to seafarers and their families, with a ticketed record of each complaint.
Practical actors, but not law: the seafarers' unions, and the ITF inspectorate, which in practice recovers a great deal of unpaid wage.

blocks.p: No circular number, named cell, named office, forum or tribunal is asserted here, and no section of the 2025 Act is cited by number. The machinery above is stated at the level at which it is verifiable.

blocks.h: 7. The thread that joins the four limbs

blocks.p: Close by connecting them, because the connection is the understanding the examiner is testing.

The flag State certifies and the port State verifies - and both can be entirely satisfied while a seafarer sits unpaid on a properly certified ship. Certification catches systems; it does not catch individual wrongs. What closes that gap is the complaint - and that is exactly why a complaint is not merely a welfare mechanism but one of the four triggers that entitles an officer to stop treating the certificate as conclusive, carry out a more detailed inspection, and if necessary detain the ship.

Limb (d) is the same thread followed to its Indian end. India cannot inspect a foreign ship in a foreign port; what it can do is regulate the agent who is within its reach, and make that agent answerable for the engagement it arranged.

Four limbs at four marks each. The framing section is short and buys structure for the whole answer by establishing the Articles / Regulations / Part A / Part B architecture, which every limb afterwards uses without re-explaining.

Limb (b) is given two numbered sections because the on-board and onshore procedures are separate machinery with separate rules. Running them together is the commonest way to lose half that limb. The closing section is worth writing even under time pressure: it is where the candidate shows he understands why the pieces are arranged as they are, and it takes four lines.

ul: Reciting the Paris MoU list of detainable deficiencies. That is a different instrument. The MLC publishes no list and gives two grounds.
Saying Part I of the DMLC is drawn up by the shipowner. Part I is the competent authority's; Part II is the shipowner's.
Describing port State inspection as a full audit. The certificate is prima facie evidence; the ordinary inspection is a document review.
Treating the on-board procedure as compulsory before any external complaint. The lowest-level preference is expressly without prejudice to direct complaint to the master or to external authorities.
Answering limb (d) as though India were the flag State. For most Indian seafarers it is not; the operative head is labour-supplying responsibility.
Inventing an Indian forum. No cell, tribunal, circular or section number should appear.
Answering from the pre-2024 text. The 2022 amendments have been in force since 23 December 2024 and are law at this sitting.
Citing the 2025 amendments as current obligations. Shore leave without a visa and key-worker recognition are adopted, with entry into force expected on 23 December 2027.
Citing the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. It was repealed on 15 March 2026.
Part B is guidance, not the measure of compliance. A port State inspection is limited to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A.
The MLC is amended by the ILO's own tripartite machinery, not by IMO tacit acceptance. Candidates habitually import the IMO procedure.

blocks.p: A seafarer's problem is that the people who owe him things are a long way away and the ship keeps moving. His employer may be registered in one country, the ship flagged in a second, the crew agent in a third, and he himself may be in a port belonging to none of them. So the Convention that protects him is built to answer one question over and over: when this man has a grievance, who can actually do something about it, and can he reach them?
The design is layered, and the four parts of this question are simply four layers of the same structure.

First, the flag State - the country whose flag the ship flies - has to run a real system of checking and certifying, and the ship carries paper saying it passed. Second, any port she visits may look at her too, and the visiting inspector normally starts by believing the paper, because otherwise the certificate would be worthless. Third, because paper can be true and the ship still bad, there is a route for the seafarer himself to raise something: on board first, quietly, to the people who can fix it fastest - and if that fails, to an official ashore who can escalate it right up to the international body itself. And fourth, if what the inspector finds is bad enough, the ship can simply be stopped from sailing.

The idea worth holding onto is the one that connects the middle two. A ship can be fully certified, inspected and lawful on paper while a seafarer sits on board unpaid. Certificates catch systems; they do not catch individual wrongs. The complaint is what closes that gap - which is exactly why a complaint is itself one of the things that entitles an inspector to stop believing the paper and start looking properly.

The last part asks where an Indian seafarer stands. The answer turns on a fact about the trade: most Indian seafarers sail on foreign ships, so India is usually not the flag State and cannot inspect the vessel. What India can reach is the agent who put the man on board - which is why the licensing of crewing agents does more practical work for an Indian seafarer than the flag State machinery ever will.

steps.title: Which text applies, and how the Convention is built
points: An ILO instrument, in force 20 August 2013 - the fourth pillar alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW
Articles, Regulations, Code Part A Standards (MANDATORY) and Code Part B Guidelines (guidance). Five Titles, of which TITLE 5 is compliance and enforcement
At this sitting the operative text is AS AMENDED THROUGH THE 2022 SET (in force 23 December 2024). The 2025 amendments are ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE - expected 23 December 2027

steps.title: Flag State and port State responsibilities
points: FLAG: an effective system of inspection and certification; recognized organizations may be authorised but the flag State REMAINS FULLY RESPONSIBLE; inspection interval shall in no case exceed three years; inspectors may PROHIBIT SAILING
The Maritime Labour Certificate and the DMLC at 500 GT on international voyages - five years, with an intermediate inspection; DMLC PART I BY THE COMPETENT AUTHORITY, PART II BY THE SHIPOWNER

PORT: any foreign ship may be inspected, but the certificate and DMLC are ACCEPTED AS PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE, so the ordinary inspection is a document review, limited to the Articles, Regulations and Part A only. NO MORE FAVOURABLE TREATMENT for ships of non-ratifying States

steps.title: The on-board complaint procedure
points: Fair, effective and expeditious handling, with resolution sought AT THE LOWEST LEVEL - but WITHOUT PREJUDICE to the right to complain directly to the master or to external authorities
A copy of the procedure to EVERY seafarer, with contact information and the name of an IMPARTIAL ADVISER on board; the right to be accompanied or represented
VICTIMIZATION FOR FILING A COMPLAINT IS PROHIBITED AND PENALIZED - the provision that makes all the rest usable

steps.title: The onshore complaint-handling procedure
points: A complaint may be made to an AUTHORIZED OFFICER in the port; he seeks resolution at ship level first, and may make an initial investigation
If unresolved, the FLAG STATE IS NOTIFIED for advice and a corrective plan of action, with a copy to the shipowners' and seafarers' organisations in the port State
If still unresolved, a report goes to the DIRECTOR-GENERAL OF THE ILO. THE SOURCE OF THE COMPLAINT IS KEPT CONFIDENTIAL throughout

steps.title: Detainable deficiencies under flag State and port State intervention
points: THE CONVENTION PUBLISHES NO LIST. It gives TWO GROUNDS: conditions CLEARLY HAZARDOUS to the safety, health or security of seafarers; or a SERIOUS OR REPEATED BREACH of the requirements, including seafarers' rights
FLAG STATE: inspectors may PROHIBIT THE SHIP LEAVING PORT for a serious breach or significant danger (Standard A5.1.4) - same two grounds, own ship, any port
They are reached only through a MORE DETAILED INSPECTION, opened on one of four triggers: documents missing or invalid; CLEAR GROUNDS; the flag changed to avoid compliance; or A COMPLAINT
Then rectification, or an accepted plan of action; the flag State is NOTIFIED FORTHWITH; and COMPENSATION IS PAYABLE FOR UNDUE DETENTION OR DELAY

steps.title: Grievance redressal for Indian seafarers
points: LAYER 1 - the Convention's own route, which every Indian seafarer already has: on board, to the master, to the flag State, to an authorized officer in port, to the Director-General of the ILO

LAYER 2 - what India can actually reach. India is flag State for Indian ships; but MOST INDIAN SEAFARERS SERVE ON FOREIGN FLAGS, so the operative head is LABOUR-SUPPLYING responsibility, with the licensing of recruitment and placement services, the NO-FEES RULE and a system of protection against the agent's failure

LAYER 3 - the domestic frame: the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (in force 15 March 2026), the shipping master for engagement, discharge and wage disputes, and the DGMA (formerly DG Shipping) with its e-Navik grievance mechanism. Unions and the ITF inspectorate are practical actors, NOT law

steps.title: The thread that joins the four limbs
points: Flag State certifies and port State verifies - and both can be satisfied while a seafarer sits unpaid on a fully certified ship
What closes that gap is THE COMPLAINT, which is why a complaint is also one of the four triggers for a more detailed inspection and hence a route to detention
Limb d) is the same thread followed to its Indian end: regulate the agent who is within reach, because the foreign owner is not

The MLC publishes NO LIST of detainable deficiencies - it gives two grounds, reached only through a more detailed inspection opened on one of four triggers. retrieval_cards.prompt: The DMLC has two parts. Who draws up each, and what does each contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I is drawn up by the COMPETENT AUTHORITY of the flag State and identifies the national requirements implementing the Convention. Part II is drawn up by the SHIPOWNER and sets out the measures adopted on that ship to ensure ongoing compliance between inspections. Candidates habitually reverse them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what grounds may a port State detain a ship under the MLC, and how is that point reached?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Convention publishes no list. Two grounds: conditions clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers; or a serious or repeated breach of the requirements, including seafarers' rights. They are reached only through a MORE DETAILED INSPECTION, opened on one of four triggers - documents not produced, not maintained or falsely maintained; clear grounds; the flag changed to avoid compliance; or a complaint.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Trace the onshore complaint-handling procedure from the seafarer to its highest rung.
retrieval_cards.answer: The seafarer complains to an authorized officer in the port. The officer makes an initial investigation and seeks resolution at ship level. If unresolved, he notifies the flag State, seeking advice and a corrective plan of action, copying the shipowners' and seafarers' organisations in the port State. If still unresolved, the report and the flag State's response go to the Director-General of the International Labour Office. The source of the complaint is kept confidential throughout.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Must a seafarer exhaust the on-board complaint procedure before going to anyone else?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Convention expresses a preference for resolution at the lowest level, but that preference is expressly WITHOUT PREJUDICE to the seafarer's right to complain directly to the master and directly to external authorities such as the flag State administration or an authorized officer in a port of call. Victimization for filing a complaint is prohibited and must be penalized.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must a port State accept the Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC as prima facie evidence?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because without that presumption the certificate would carry no value and every port would re-audit every ship. The presumption makes the ORDINARY port State inspection a document review, limited to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A of the Code, and it is displaced only when one of the four triggers for a more detailed inspection is present.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which MLC responsibility is the operative one for most Indian seafarers, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: LABOUR-SUPPLYING responsibility, the third limb of Title 5. Most Indian seafarers serve on foreign-flag ships, so India is neither flag State nor usually port State and cannot inspect the vessel. What it can reach is the recruitment and placement service that put the seafarer on board - licensing it, requiring registers and verification of employment agreements, enforcing the prohibition on charging recruitment fees, and requiring a system of protection to compensate the seafarer for the agent's failure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which text of the MLC is operative at an October 2026 sitting, and what is adopted but not in force?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Convention as amended through the 2022 amendments, which entered into force on 23 December 2024 (social connectivity, free drinking water, sized PPE, food and catering, repatriation of remains). The 2025 amendments (shore leave without a visa, key-worker recognition) are ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE - expected 23 December 2027.
retrieval_cards.why: Edition is the commonest silent error on this Convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the MLC Code amended, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: By the ILO's own machinery - the Special Tripartite Committee, with approval by the International Labour Conference - not by IMO tacit acceptance. Candidates habitually import the IMO amendment procedure, which produces a wrong account of how and when a change becomes binding.

blocks.h: (a) The bill of lading and its three legal functions
1. What a bill of lading is

blocks.p: A bill of lading is the document issued by or on behalf of the carrier - signed by the master or the carrier's agent - acknowledging that goods have been received for shipment or shipped on board a named vessel, for carriage to a named destination and delivery there to the person entitled.

Under the Hague-Visby Rules the carrier must, on the shipper's demand, issue a bill showing the leading marks, the number of packages or the quantity or weight, and the apparent order and condition of the goods. India's governing statutes changed in 2025: the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (Act 18 of 2025) and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025), both in force from 10 September 2025, repealed the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925. The 2025 COGSA's Schedule applies the Hague-Visby Rules by statute.

blocks.h: 2. Function 1 - a receipt for the goods

blocks.p: The bill is the carrier's receipt: it records what was shipped and in what apparent order and condition. A clean bill carries no adverse remark; a claused bill notes defects. Under the Hague-Visby Rules the bill is prima facie evidence of receipt as described, and conclusive once it has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith. That is why the master must not sign a clean bill for goods he knows are damaged.

blocks.h: 3. Function 2 - evidence of the contract of carriage

blocks.p: The contract of carriage is usually concluded before the bill is issued - on booking, or under a charterparty - so between the original parties the bill is evidence of the contract's terms, not the contract itself. Once it is transferred to a lawful holder, such as a consignee or endorsee, the bill becomes the contract between that holder and the carrier, and statute transfers to the holder the rights - and liabilities - of suit. In India that transfer is governed by the Bills of Lading Act, 2025.

The bill is a document of title: holding it represents the right to take delivery of the goods, so the goods can be sold or pledged while still at sea by transferring the bill. The carrier, in return, delivers only against presentation of an original bill. This function is what lets banks finance trade under letters of credit, holding the bill as security.
One caveat the examiner may test: the full document-of-title function belongs to a negotiable bill - an order or bearer bill. A straight bill is not negotiable, as part (b) shows.

blocks.h: (b) Straight, order and bearer bills - and how delivery is effected

blocks.p: A straight bill names a specific consignee and contains no words such as 'to order'. It is not negotiable: it cannot be transferred to anyone else by endorsement, so it suits sales where the goods will not be resold in transit, or shipments between related companies.

Delivery: to the named consignee only, on proof of identity. Whether the carrier may deliver without the original being presented depends on the governing law and the bill's terms; English law, for example, has held that an original must be presented. The safe practice is to deliver against an original straight bill unless the bill expressly provides otherwise.

An order bill is made out 'to order', 'to the order of the shipper' or 'to the order of' a named party such as the buyer's bank. It is negotiable: it passes by endorsement and delivery. A special endorsement names the next holder; an endorsement in blank (signature only) turns it into a bearer bill.
Delivery: to the person who presents an original bill bearing an unbroken chain of endorsements down to himself. This is the normal bill for documentary credits and for cargo sold in transit.
A bearer bill is made out 'to bearer', or is an order bill endorsed in blank. It passes by delivery alone - whoever physically holds it is the holder.
Delivery: to whoever presents an original. It is the easiest bill to transfer and the most dangerous: a lost or stolen bearer bill can be used to take the cargo, so it is rarely used deliberately.

blocks.h: 1. The Convention's definition of pollution, and what makes it unusually wide

blocks.p: UNCLOS article 1(1)(4) defines "pollution of the marine environment" as the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as: harm to living resources and marine life; hazards to human health; hindrance to marine activities, including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea; impairment of quality for use of sea water; and reduction of amenities.
Five features of that wording earn marks, and each should be stated as a point:

ol: "By man" - a natural seep or a volcanic discharge is not pollution under the Convention, however damaging.
"Directly or indirectly" - a river carrying industrial waste to the sea is caught, so the polluting act need not happen at sea at all.
"Substances or energy" - heat, noise and radiation are pollution. This is the element most candidates omit and it is the one that makes the definition modern.
"Results or is likely to result" - no damage need have occurred. Likelihood is enough, which is what allows preventive regulation.
"Reduction of amenities" - purely aesthetic and recreational harm counts. Oil on a beach is pollution even where nothing is killed.

blocks.p: Note finally that the definition is source-neutral. Nothing in it mentions ships. Ships are one source among land-based sources, dumping, seabed activities and the atmosphere, and that is why the coastal State's obligations are structured source by source.

blocks.h: 2. The general obligation, and why it is not confined to any zone

blocks.p: Article 192 states the whole of Part XII in one sentence: States have the obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment. It is free-standing and not zone-limited - the rest of the Convention allocates rights zone by zone, but this imposes a duty across all of them, including the high seas.

Article 193 then makes the balance explicit: States have the sovereign right to exploit their natural resources pursuant to their environmental policies and in accordance with their duty to protect and preserve the marine environment. Development is permitted; it is not unconditioned.
Article 194 is the operative obligation:

ul: 194(1) - all measures necessary to prevent, reduce and control pollution from any source, using the best practicable means at their disposal and in accordance with their capabilities, endeavouring to harmonize policies. Note that the standard is expressly capability-relative.
194(2) - activities under a State's jurisdiction or control must not cause damage by pollution to other States, and pollution from incidents under its control must not spread beyond its zones.

194(3)(b) - for vessels specifically: preventing accidents, dealing with emergencies, ensuring safety of operations, preventing intentional and unintentional discharges, and regulating design, construction, equipment, operation and manning.
194(5) - measures to protect rare or fragile ecosystems and the habitat of depleted, threatened or endangered species.

blocks.p: Two short articles complete the frame and are easy marks. Article 195 forbids a State, in taking measures, from transferring damage or hazards from one area to another, or transforming one type of pollution into another - so scrubbing a stack emission into the sea is not compliance. Article 196 covers harmful technologies and the introduction of alien or new species, which is the treaty root of ballast water and biofouling control.
Part XII deals with pollution source by source, and the coastal State's freedom of action differs sharply between them:

blocks.p: Article 211 is the one that matters for ships, and its internal structure is the answer to "key features":

ul: 211(1) - rules and standards are established through the competent international organization, that is the IMO, and are re-examined from time to time.
211(2) - a flag State's own laws must have at least the same effect as those international standards. Stricter for your own ships, yes; laxer, no.
211(4) - in the territorial sea a coastal State may legislate for foreign vessels including those in innocent passage, but such laws shall not hamper innocent passage.
211(5) - in the exclusive economic zone it may legislate only conforming to and giving effect to generally accepted international rules. It cannot invent its own standard.

211(6) - the one escape route: for a particular, clearly defined area of its EEZ where the international rules are inadequate, it may submit scientific and technical evidence to the IMO; the IMO determines within 12 months; the measures bind foreign vessels only 15 months after submission; and they may never impose design, construction, manning or equipment standards other than the generally accepted international ones.

blocks.p: That last prohibition is the single most quotable limit in Part XII. It is why a coastal State can impose a discharge or routeing requirement but cannot demand a different hull, and it is the legal basis on which Special Areas and Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas are created through the IMO rather than declared unilaterally.

blocks.h: 4. The coastal State's obligations - enforcement, and its limits

blocks.p: Rule-making and enforcement are separately allocated, and confusing them is the commonest error on this question.

ul: Article 217 - the flag State. The primary enforcement duty: compliance by ships of its flag wherever the violation occurs.

Article 218 - the port State. Where a ship is voluntarily in port, proceedings may be taken for a discharge outside that State's own waters - a jurisdiction that exists nowhere else in the Convention.

Article 220 - the coastal State, and its powers are deliberately graded: proceedings where the ship is voluntarily in port for a violation in its territorial sea or EEZ (220(1)); on clear grounds for a territorial-sea violation, physical inspection and, where the evidence warrants, proceedings including detention (220(2)); and for an EEZ violation, first only the power to require information - identity, port of registry, last and next port of call (220(3)) - escalating to inspection and then to detention as the evidence and the gravity of the discharge increase.

Article 221 - after a maritime casualty, the right to take and enforce measures beyond the territorial sea, proportionate to the actual or threatened damage, to protect the coastline and related interests including fishing, where major harmful consequences may reasonably be expected. The article carries its own definition of maritime casualty.
Article 235 - States are responsible for fulfilling their international obligations and must ensure recourse for prompt and adequate compensation for pollution damage.

blocks.p: The safeguards in section 7 of Part XII then constrain how all of this is exercised. The shape of the coastal State's position is therefore: a duty everywhere, rule-making power that narrows as you move seaward, and enforcement power that is graded by evidence and by seriousness. And article 235 is the bridge to the second limb - the compensation regime exists because UNCLOS requires that recourse.

blocks.h: 5. Why the oil pollution compensation regime has three tiers

blocks.p: Before listing the tiers, say why there are tiers. A major tanker spill can cost more than any shipowner or his insurer could reasonably carry. Unlimited liability would have made tankers uninsurable; leaving victims uncompensated was politically and legally unacceptable. The compromise reached was that the shipowner is liable strictly but with a limit, and the balance is placed on the cargo interest - those who receive the oil.
The defining idea of the regime is therefore that the cost of an oil spill is shared between the ship and the cargo. Every feature below follows from it.

ul: There is a right of direct action against the insurer, so the victim is not defeated by the owner's insolvency.
The owner may limit his liability by reference to the tonnage of the ship. No figure is given here - the limits are amended over time and every figure carries a date.
He loses the right to limit if the damage resulted from his personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result.

The exceptions are narrow: act of war; a wholly exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party's intentional act; or the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids.

blocks.p: Three points here separate a good answer from a list:

ol: The cargo interest pays for tiers two and three - not the shipowner and not governments. The Funds are financed by the oil receivers in the member States. This is the fact most candidates get wrong.
The tiers are cumulative and sequential, each with its own overall ceiling for any one incident, and each tier is reached only when the one below it is exhausted or unavailable.

Tier three is optional. A State must already be a member of the 1992 Fund and must separately accede to the 2003 Protocol. So the compensation available for the same casualty depends on where it happens.

blocks.p: Note the answer to "certification required by ship under each tier" precisely: only tier one produces a certificate carried by the ship. Saying so, and explaining why - the Funds are financed ashore, not by the ship - is worth more than inventing two more certificates.

blocks.h: 8. What the three tiers do NOT cover - and the trap

ul: The regime is about persistent oil carried in bulk as cargo - in substance, the laden or residue-carrying tanker case. It is not a general marine pollution compensation scheme.

Bunker oil spilled from a non-tanker is the Bunkers Convention 2001: strict liability on a wider group of owners, compulsory insurance and a certificate, but a single tier with no fund behind it. A candidate who offers Bunkers as one of the three tiers has misread the question.
Hazardous and noxious substances have their own convention, which is not in force at this sitting. It cannot be cited as a tier or as current law.
Geography matters. The tiers respond only in States party, and the third only where that State has opted in.

In India, domestic effect to the civil liability and fund regimes is given through the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, in force since 15 March 2026 (it repealed the 1958 Act), and rules made under it. India is a Party to CLC 1992 and the Fund Convention 1992 but not to the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003, so in Indian waters only the first two tiers respond.

blocks.p: Close by joining the two limbs, because the examiner printed them together: UNCLOS article 235 obliges States to ensure recourse for prompt and adequate compensation for pollution damage, and the three tiers are how that obligation is discharged for oil. The first limb states the duty; the second shows the machinery.

Two limbs, no printed marks, and a very wide subject. The risk is not ignorance - most candidates know something about UNCLOS and something about CLC - it is drift: writing a general essay on marine pollution and never answering either printed instruction. The route defends against that by anchoring each limb on the words the examiner actually used.

Limb A prints two demands - "define" and "discuss the key features of obligations of coastal states". Definition is a quotation task: reproduce article 1(1)(4) as closely as you can and then dissect it, because every element of it is a scoring proposition. Obligations is a structure task: the marks are in showing that the Convention allocates rule-making and enforcement separately, and that the coastal State's freedom narrows as it moves seaward.

Limb B prints three demands and they are easy to leave one out: who pays, the source of funds, and the certification required by the ship, in each case. Three demands times three tiers is nine propositions, and they are best written as a table. Step 5 - why there are tiers at all - is what turns the table from a memorised list into an explanation, and step 8 is where the examiner separates candidates by asking, in effect, what the regime is not.

blocks.h: The definition is worth learning word for word

blocks.p: Very few provisions repay verbatim memory as well as article 1(1)(4), because the marks are distributed across its clauses. If you can write "the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as..." you have earned several propositions before you have explained anything.

The five deleterious effects are: harm to living resources and marine life; hazards to human health; hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea; impairment of quality for use of sea water; and reduction of amenities. Reduction of amenities and or energy are the two most frequently omitted, and both are distinctive enough to be noticed.

blocks.h: Rule-making and enforcement are different questions

blocks.p: Candidates routinely answer "what are the coastal State's obligations" by listing enforcement powers. The Convention separates them, and saying so is itself a scoring point. Rule-making runs 207 land-based, 210 dumping, 211 vessels, 212 atmosphere - and the coastal State's discretion is widest for land-based sources and narrowest for ships. Enforcement runs 217 flag, 218 port, 220 coastal, 221 casualties - and the coastal State's power is graded rather than absolute.

The reason for the asymmetry is worth one sentence: a State may regulate its own territory as it likes, but a ship is a moving object subject to another State's flag, so uniform international standards are the only workable basis. That is why article 211 keeps referring back to the competent international organization.

blocks.h: The 12 and 15 month periods in article 211(6)

blocks.p: If you can carry two numbers into this answer, carry these. Where a coastal State wants special mandatory measures for a clearly defined area of its EEZ, it communicates to the IMO with scientific and technical evidence; the IMO determines within 12 months; and the laws become applicable to foreign vessels only 15 months after the submission. They may never impose design, construction, manning or equipment standards beyond the generally accepted international ones. That paragraph is the legal skeleton of the Special Area and PSSA machinery, and quoting the two periods proves the Convention was opened.

ul: Paraphrasing the definition loosely and losing "or energy", "indirectly", "is likely to result" and "reduction of amenities" - four separate propositions gone.
Answering limb A entirely with enforcement powers and never mentioning the rule-making obligations.
Treating article 192 as applying only inside national zones. It is not zone-limited.
Offering the Bunkers Convention 2001 as one of the three tiers. It is a separate, single-tier regime for bunkers from non-tankers.
Offering the HNS Convention as a tier, or describing it as in force. It is not in force at this sitting.
Saying the Funds are financed by shipowners or by governments. They are financed by receivers of contributing oil.
Inventing a Fund certificate or a Supplementary Fund certificate carried by the ship. Only tier one produces a ship's certificate.
Quoting SDR limits from memory. They are amended over time and a stale figure is worse than none.
Writing that the coastal State may impose its own construction standards on foreign ships in its EEZ. Article 211(6) expressly forbids it.
Forgetting that the owner loses the right to limit for his own intentional or reckless conduct with knowledge.
"Is noise pollution?" Yes - the definition says substances or energy. So is waste heat.
"Must damage have occurred?" No - 'results or is likely to result'.

"Can a coastal State demand a double hull in its EEZ?" No. Article 211(6) permits special measures for a defined area but not design, construction, manning or equipment standards beyond the generally accepted international ones.
"Who may be sued under CLC 92?" The registered owner, and liability is channelled to him - not the manager, charterer, crew, pilot or salvor.
"Who pays for tiers two and three?" Receivers of contributing oil. Say cargo, not ship.
"What does the ship carry for tier two?" Nothing. Only the CLC certificate is a ship's document.
"Is the third tier available everywhere?" No - it is optional, and requires 1992 Fund membership first.
"What links the two limbs?" Article 235 - the duty to ensure recourse for prompt and adequate compensation.
Define pollution under UNCLOS. Give the article. Article 1(1)(4).
Which article states the general obligation? 192. And what qualifies the right to exploit resources? 193.
Which article deals with pollution from vessels? 211. What standard must national law meet? At least the same effect as the generally accepted international rules.
What can a coastal State do about a suspected discharge in its EEZ? Require information first; inspect on clear grounds; detain only where the evidence and the gravity warrant it - article 220.
What may a State do after a casualty outside its territorial sea? Measures proportionate to the actual or threatened damage - article 221.
Name the three tiers. CLC 1992, the 1992 Fund, the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003.
Who is strictly liable under tier one and can he limit? The registered owner; yes, by tonnage, unless the damage resulted from his personal intentional or reckless act with knowledge.

What certificate does the ship carry, and who issues it? A certificate of insurance or other financial security under CLC 92, issued or certified by the State, on the strength of the insurer's blue card.
Is the Bunkers Convention one of the tiers? No - separate regime, one tier, no fund.

blocks.p: For limb A, DEFINE - DUTY - RULES - ENFORCE. Inside the definition, MAN, INDIRECT, ENERGY, LIKELY, AMENITIES - the five words that carry the marks. Inside rule-making, walk seaward: LAND (207) - DUMP (210) - SHIPS (211) - AIR (212), discretion shrinking as you go. Inside enforcement, FLAG - PORT - COASTAL - CASUALTY, that is 217, 218, 220, 221.

For limb B, SHIP - CARGO - CARGO. Tier one is the ship and its insurer; tiers two and three are both the cargo receivers. Then the three demands in every row: WHO PAYS - WHERE FROM - WHAT PAPER. And remember the answer to the third column is certificate, none, none.

questions.understand_first: Strip the two limbs down and they are one idea seen twice. The first asks what the law of the sea means by pollution and what it therefore requires of the State whose coastline is at risk; the second asks who actually pays when the pollution happens anyway. The definition is deliberately enormous - anything a person puts into the sea, whether a substance or merely energy such as heat or noise, that is likely to do harm, even if no harm has yet occurred. Because it is that wide, the duty it creates has to be split up, and the way the Convention splits it is the real content of the first limb: a State has almost a free hand over what it does on its own land, and almost none over what it demands of a foreign ship, because a ship moves and belongs to somebody else. So the rules for ships are made through the international organisation, and the coastal State's power to enforce them grows as the evidence and the seriousness grow. The second limb follows from the last piece of the first: having imposed a duty, the Convention also requires that victims can actually recover. For oil that recovery is built in layers, and the reason it is layered is that no single shipowner could carry the cost of a bad spill and no insurer would write unlimited cover. So the cost is shared between the ship and the cargo - the owner pays first, strictly but only up to a limit, and beyond that the people who receive the oil pay through funds they finance. Once you see that the whole scheme is ship-then-cargo, the details stop being a list to memorise.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: UNCLOS article 1(1)(4) defines pollution of the marine environment as the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water and reduction of amenities. Article 192 imposes the general obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment, and article 211 requires that rules for vessel-source pollution be established through the competent international organization, with national law having at least the same effect.
quick_revision.major_trap: Two traps, one in each limb. In limb A, answering "the obligations of coastal states" with a list of enforcement powers and never mentioning the rule-making obligations under articles 207 to 212 - and in particular missing that the coastal State's discretion is widest for land-based sources and narrowest for ships, and that article 211(6) forbids it from imposing design, construction, manning or equipment standards on foreign ships even in a special area. In limb B, offering the Bunkers Convention 2001 as one of the three tiers, saying the Funds are financed by shipowners or governments rather than by receivers of contributing oil, and inventing Fund certificates carried by the ship - only tier one produces a ship's certificate. And quote no SDR figure: the limits are amended over time and a remembered number is probably a superseded one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the UNCLOS pollution and three-tiers question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The definition and what makes it wide. 2 The general obligation, not zone-limited. 3 Coastal State rule-making, source by source. 4 Coastal State enforcement, graded. 5 Why there are three tiers at all. 6 Tier one, the shipowner. 7 Tiers two and three, the Funds. 8 What the tiers do not cover.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 5 and 8 are what lift limb B out of a memorised list; step 3 is where most candidates lose limb A.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define pollution of the marine environment under UNCLOS, and give the article.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 1(1)(4): the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water, and reduction of amenities.
retrieval_cards.why: The marks are distributed across the clauses, so a loose paraphrase loses several propositions at once.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which four elements of the UNCLOS definition are most often omitted, and why does each matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: 'By man' - a natural seep is not pollution. 'Indirectly' - a river carrying waste to the sea is caught. 'Or energy' - heat, noise and radiation are pollution. 'Is likely to result' - no damage need have occurred, which is what permits preventive regulation. A fifth, 'reduction of amenities', makes purely aesthetic harm count.
retrieval_cards.why: Each is a separate scoring proposition and each is distinctive enough for an examiner to notice its absence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the coastal State's rule-making obligations from its enforcement powers under Part XII.
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule-making runs source by source - article 207 land-based, 210 dumping, 211 vessels, 212 atmosphere - and the coastal State's discretion is widest for land-based sources and narrowest for ships, where it must act through the IMO and legislate only to at least the same effect. Enforcement is separately allocated - 217 flag, 218 port, 220 coastal, 221 after a casualty - and the coastal State's power is graded by evidence and gravity.
retrieval_cards.why: Answering 'obligations' with enforcement alone is the commonest way to lose half of limb A.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does article 211(6) allow a coastal State to do in its EEZ, on what timetable, and what does it forbid?
retrieval_cards.answer: For a particular, clearly defined area where the international rules are inadequate, it may communicate to the IMO with supporting scientific and technical evidence; the IMO determines within 12 months; the resulting laws apply to foreign vessels only 15 months after submission. It may never impose design, construction, manning or equipment standards other than generally accepted international ones.
retrieval_cards.why: The two periods prove the Convention was opened, and the prohibition is the legal skeleton of Special Areas and PSSAs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How are a coastal State's enforcement powers graded under article 220?
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the ship is voluntarily in port, proceedings may be instituted for a violation in the territorial sea or EEZ. For a territorial-sea violation, on clear grounds, physical inspection and, where the evidence warrants, proceedings including detention. For an EEZ violation, on clear grounds, first only a power to require information - identity, port of registry, last and next port of call - escalating to inspection and then detention as the evidence and the seriousness of the discharge increase.
retrieval_cards.why: The grading is the point of the article; describing it as a single power to detain misstates the Convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three tiers of oil pollution compensation, and say who is responsible for payment in each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Tier one, CLC 1992 - the registered owner of the ship, strictly, with liability channelled to him. Tier two, the Fund Convention 1992 - the 1992 IOPC Fund. Tier three, the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003 - the Supplementary Fund. The tiers are cumulative and sequential, each reached only when the one below is exhausted or unavailable.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks 'in each case' who is responsible, so all three must be named separately.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does the money for tiers two and three actually come from?
retrieval_cards.answer: From levies on receivers of contributing oil - crude oil and heavy fuel oil received by sea above a threshold quantity in a State Party. The cargo interest funds both Funds, not the shipowner and not governments. Tier three additionally requires that the State has opted into the 2003 Protocol, having first joined the 1992 Fund.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single most commonly wrong statement on the question, and it is also the idea that explains the whole regime.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What certification does the ship carry under each of the three tiers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only under tier one. A certificate of insurance or other financial security under CLC 1992, issued or certified by the State on the strength of the insurer's blue card, carried on board by ships carrying persistent oil in bulk as cargo. Neither Fund tier produces a ship's certificate, because the Funds are financed ashore by cargo receivers rather than by the ship.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks specifically about certification per tier, and the correct answer is certificate, none, none - with the reason.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the Bunkers Convention 2001 one of the three tiers?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is a separate regime for pollution by bunker oil from ships other than tankers carrying persistent oil as cargo - strict liability, compulsory insurance and a certificate, but a single tier with no fund behind it. The HNS Convention is likewise not a tier, and is not in force at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: Offering Bunkers as a tier is the classic misread, and naming the boundary correctly is itself worth marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What connects the two printed limbs of this question?
retrieval_cards.answer: UNCLOS article 235. Having imposed the duty to protect and preserve the marine environment, the Convention also requires States to ensure that recourse is available for prompt and adequate compensation for pollution damage. The three tiers are the machinery by which that obligation is discharged for oil.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner printed the two limbs together; saying why converts two half-answers into one argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why should you quote no SDR figure in this answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the CLC tonnage-band limits and both Fund ceilings are amended by tacit acceptance over time, so every figure carries a date and a number recalled from a textbook is likely to be superseded. The question asks who pays, from what source and against what certificate - none of which requires a figure.
retrieval_cards.why: A confidently stated stale number reads worse to an examiner than an accurate description with no number in it.
